result.reason: I found no single product that kills this idea, but free and paid substitutes already cover much of the core job. ICICI's free Trade Online "Trade OneView" dashboard shows outstanding export bills and is linked to EDPMS, so exporters can match payments to open entries there. ICEGATE has a free EDPMS status lookup by shipping bill number. Kyzer Software sells EDPMS/IDPMS software to banks that includes a portal for their corporate clients. The trigger looks real: secondary sources agree on the 9-month rule and the 22 Sep 2026 amendment, and a May 2026 Customs notice ties export incentives to EDPMS reconciliation. Still open: whether a firm banking with several banks would pay for one cross-bank tracker, and whether Tally add-ons already offer one. My Tally search found nothing.

result.competitor:
I found no dedicated self-serve cess and Form XV-XVIII tool aimed at small builders. What exists:
- TeamLease RegTech says it provides support for BOCW cess assessment and deposit, plus statutory registers and returns. It pairs its RegTrack software with managed services and serves enterprises (450+ clients).
- Simpliance is a general labour-law compliance tool from Rs 20,000 a year, with no BOCW module that I could confirm.
- Patron Accounting and ALP Consulting are done-for-you services.
- The state side covers payment and registration: Tripura has a cess deposit portal (labourcess.tripura.gov.in), Assam takes cess through EGRAS, Haryana has an online cess calculator and Form 1 filing, West Bengal has online registration, and Shram Suvidha handles central registration.
- The main thing that weakens the idea is not a rival product: local authorities collect the cess at plan approval and government buyers deduct it at source, so the money side is largely handled already.
result.duty:
The duty is real and in force. BOCW cess now falls under Chapter VIII (ss.100-108) of the Code on Social Security, 2020. The Code took effect on 21 Nov 2025 according to Taxmann and other commentary; I did not check the Gazette for that date. S.O. 2322(E) of 8 May 2026 sets the rate at 1% of construction cost, excluding land, and supersedes the 1996 notification S.O. 2899. Under the rules as Taxmann reports them:
- Rule 41: advance payment on a self-assessment certified by a chartered engineer, using the PWD/CPWD schedule of rates or the RERA cost (Form XVI). Projects over one year can pay in yearly instalments.
- Form XV within 60 days of starting work or paying cess; changes within 30 days.
- Form XVII for stoppage or reduction of work, within 60 days.
- Form XVIII return and final self-assessment (s.103) within 60 days of completing each project.
- The assessing officer can scrutinise a return only if the self-assessed cess exceeds Rs 10 lakh, and must act within 180 days or the self-assessment becomes final.
- Interest is 1% a month. Penalty is up to the amount of cess (s.104).

In practice, cess on government or PSU work is deducted from contractor bills, and in many states (e.g. J&K, Meghalaya, Odisha) the local authority collects 1% upfront when it approves the building plan. That leaves small private builders with mainly the returns and final adjustment. Taxmann does not mention the 10-worker threshold in the claim. I could not confirm whether each state board has adopted the Code rules and the new forms.
result.market: I found no national count. CAG reports point to low registration and enforcement. Rajasthan registered only 2,464 establishments between 2017 and 2022, 40% of them late. CAG audits of Jharkhand and Maharashtra also found weak cess collection. The number of firms that actually file is probably small, in the low tens of thousands nationally, and many are covered by plan-approval collection. That last figure is my inference, not a sourced statistic.
result.reason: The duty is real and current: 1% cess under the Code on Social Security, S.O. 2322(E) of May 2026, with Forms XV-XVIII, a chartered engineer certificate and 1% monthly interest. No small-builder tool does the core job. But for small private builders, the money is mostly collected at plan approval by local authorities, and government work has it deducted from bills, so what is left is a few filings per project, not a monthly pain. Enforcement and registration are weak (Rajasthan: 2,464 establishments in five years), rules and portals differ by state, and the engineer certificate needs a professional. Enterprise vendors (TeamLease RegTech) and outsourcers cover larger firms. Willingness to pay and frequency look low.

result.competitor: I found no product or service built for coaching-centre registration or annual filing under the Haryana or Rajasthan rules. Generic coaching ERPs (Techjockey listings such as Coachpresso, Kumudy and G Infosoft; Jupsoft; OpenEduCat) handle enquiries, fees, batches and attendance, but I saw no regulatory-filing feature. Some of that data overlaps with the disclosures, so an ERP could add the feature cheaply. The state's own district portal handles submission. CA and consultant registration services probably exist but none came up in my searches. Competitor search: 2 queries, English only (Hindi was not tried).
result.duty: Haryana (strongest, verified): the Private Coaching Institutes (Registration and Regulation) Rules 2026 were notified on 24 Aug 2026 (S.O. 44/H.A. 12/2024/S.16/2026) under the Haryana Act 12 of 2024 and are in force. Institutes apply online on the District Authority portal; the fee is Rs 10,000 and the certificate lasts 3 years. Renewal costs Rs 5,000, must be sought 1 month before expiry and is valid for 1 year. Institutes must keep prescribed records, publish them on their website and file information with the District Authority every year. Disclosures cover fees, refund policy, batch size, teacher qualifications and facilities. Each branch registers separately. Home tuition with up to 50 students a day is exempt. Fines are reported at Rs 25,000 to Rs 1 lakh per violation plus cancellation (secondary sources disagree on the figures). Rajasthan: the bill was introduced in March 2025. One vendor blog says it was gazetted on 26 Sep 2025, with a threshold of 100 students and fines of Rs 50,000, then Rs 2 lakh, then cancellation. I found no notified rules and no live portal, so the Rajasthan rules and portal are unverified. I did not check Assam, AP, Maharashtra or Puducherry. The central 2024 MoE guidelines are only advisory: in 2025 the Ministry told Parliament that the states regulate coaching centres. Frequency is low: registration, then annual filing and yearly renewal.
result.market: Nationally there were about 68,000 coaching centres in 2024 (Dinamalar), and the Federation of Coaching Centres estimates 48,000 registered ones. No Haryana registration count exists yet. A 2024 Tribune report put Faridabad alone at over 100 centres, and another Tribune headline says 400+ there lack safety compliance. The 50- and 100-student thresholds leave out the smallest tutors. The addressable market in Haryana and Rajasthan is probably a few thousand institutes (my estimate, not a register figure).
result.reason: The duty is real and in force in Haryana, with an annual filing, a yearly renewal, website disclosure and per-branch registration. That supports a recurring service, and I found no tool that does it. But the work happens about once a year, the content is mostly static disclosures, and the rules differ by state, with Rajasthan's rules and portal still unconfirmed. Thresholds of 50 to 100 students exclude micro-tutors. The buyers are mid-size institutes that would likely hand the job to a CA or a one-off consultant, and existing coaching ERPs could add a compliance module. That makes the best fit a done-for-you registration service sold together with fee and refund policy templates. Pain and willingness to pay are moderate, and it is hard to defend as standalone SaaS.

coverage.found: Nothing displaces K06. Per a ICAR case study and Odisha district letter (2023), the DAESI diploma has been mandatory for continuing agri-input dealer licences since about 2017-18, enforced state by state (https://www.icar.org.in/index.php/hi/node/25896; https://nabarangpur.odisha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-09/Enrollement%20of%20Fertilizer%20and%20Pesticide%20Dealers%20for%20DAESI%20Training%20CDAO%20letter_0.pdf). Draft Seeds Bill 2025 would require every seed dealer/distributor to hold a state registration certificate and adds a Central Seed Traceability Portal with QR codes (https://www.civilsdaily.com/news/centre-releases-draft-seeds-bill-2025/); the minister said it would come in the 2026 budget session, but I found no confirmation it was introduced or passed. The draft Pesticides Management Bill 2025 focuses on product registration and digital licensing, with no dealer detail found (https://www.theweek.in/news/india/2026/01/07/pesticides-management-bill-explained-how-new-law-could-help-farmers-and-industry.amp.html). result.reason: The duty is real and in force in several states. Rules 6B and 6C: written appointment after background and medical checks, staff records kept for RTO and police, daily student boarding and de-boarding attendance (school and operator). Rule 10A: Digital Safety Monitoring System with VLTD, state-platform integration, CCTV, and a certified app meeting AIS-004/AIS-140 with ARAI/ICAT approval. CCTV backup must be kept at least 30 days. News reports give a three-month window, ending about mid-October 2026. The TeamLease text gives no commencement date and no penalties; a Pune police warning and RTO fitness fines (Wardha: Rs 26 lakh on 175 vehicles) show enforcement is active. Frequency is continuous or daily for records, plus annual fitness. A link between CCTV and fitness renewal was not found in the rule text.

result.reason: The duty is real. Notification MVR-0625/C.R.347/Tra-2, issued 16 Jul 2026, requires a Digital Safety Monitoring System (AIS-140 VLTD with state-platform integration, CCTV, a certified parent app with digital attendance), 30-day CCTV backup, daily boarding records, and staff verification and medical records available to RTO and police. result.duty: The FSSAI order dated 17 Dec 2025 sets a compulsory 'Scheme of Testing' for packaged drinking water (FSSR 2.10.8) and mineral water (FSSR 2.10.7), in force from 1 Jan 2026. It follows the 17 Oct 2024 notification that dropped mandatory BIS certification. Manufacturers must keep test records showing conformity across the whole production and test their source water. They must run monthly microbiological tests for E. coli, coliforms, Pseudomonas, Salmonella, Vibrio cholerae and other organisms. If a test fails, they must pull the affected batches and can resume only after 5 consecutive compliant batches. Incident records must be kept for 5 years. Foxmandal reports the category is now high-risk, which brings mandatory third-party audits. Penalties fall under the general FSS Act (penalties and/or imprisonment), but I did not verify specific amounts. I could not extract the annex text from the official PDF, so chemical and source-water testing frequencies are unverified. I found nothing saying FoSCoS requires test reports to be uploaded; my searches only showed it covers licensing, inspection and annual returns.
result.market: About 6,244 BIS-licensed packaged drinking water makers and 32 mineral water makers as of 2 Feb 2024 (parliamentary reply cited in search results). BIS reported more than 6,200 in Sept 2022, so the number has been roughly flat. A further unknown number of unlicensed RO units exist, but these are unlikely buyers. I found no 2025–26 figure.
result.reason: The duty is real and recurring. An FSSAI order dated 17 Dec 2025 created a testing scheme for packaged drinking water and mineral water, in force from 1 Jan 2026. It requires monthly microbiological tests, test records covering the whole production, and source-water testing. A failed result means withdrawing the batch and needing five compliant batches before production restarts, with records kept for five years. I found no later postponement. The market is small, though: about 6,244 licensed makers. The plants also sit on low margins, and many unlicensed units would not pay for compliance. A partial competitor exists: myFSC is an Indian app that tracks water-testing certificates and FSSAI licence expiry, with a free basic tier for small businesses. NABL labs and consultants such as Corpseed and IndiaFilings sell testing bundles. A simple test-schedule tracker is easy to build but easy to copy.

result.reason: The duty is real. Under Rule 3 of India's Radiation Protection Rules 2004, every medical and dental X-ray unit needs an AERB licence or registration through eLORA. result.duty: Real and in force. The RBI's Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026 (Notification FEMA 23(R)/(1)/2026-RB, 22 Sep 2026), confirmed on rbi.org.in, change regulation 5(1) of the principal FEMA 23(R)/2026-RB rules: 15 months becomes 9 months, and 18 months becomes 12 months for INR-invoiced exports. They take effect 1 Oct 2026, the same day the principal 2026 regulations start. The sources that seemed to conflict are about a separate change: a 5 Jun 2026 First Amendment (FEMA 23(R)/(8)/2026-RB) that took the old 2015 Export Regulations from 15 months back to 9. Both amendments say 9 months, so there is no real conflict. The 9-month clock runs from the shipment date for goods and the invoice date for services, and the AD bank can extend it. Penalties: Caution List exposure (per the Leather Council, any shipping bill open more than two years in EDPMS without an extension), with existing Caution List orders continuing under the new Regulation 13 proviso. Two secondary sources (a Mondaq summary of the regulations, Skydo) say entries up to Rs 10 lakh can be closed on the exporter's declaration, including quarterly bulk closure; I did not confirm this on rbi.org.in. Services exporters must file the EDF within 30 days of month end; this is also from secondary sources. The claim's 'advance payment or LC' consequence comes from secondary sources and was not checked against the primary text. Separately, FTP 2023 para 2.05(d) requires every IEC holder to update the IEC each year between April and June, and DGFT flagged about 59,000 IECs for deactivation in 2025.
